Age: 4 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Rapidly progressive sore throat, difficulty swallowing, noisy breathing, drooling, high fever, stridor, anxious appearance  

Analysis: All three experts identified acute epiglottitis as the most likely diagnosis based on the classic clinical triad (high fever, drooling, tripod posture) and the thumb sign on the lateral neck X‑ray. There is unanimous agreement that the airway is imminently threatened and that emergent, controlled airway protection by the most experienced anesthesiology or ENT provider is mandatory, with a surgical airway immediately available. Consensus also exists on the need for minimal stimulation, supplemental oxygen if tolerated, large‑bore IV access, isotonic fluid resuscitation, blood cultures, and continuous pulse‑oximetry and capnography monitoring.  

Points of divergence include the role of corticosteroids (Expert B recommends a routine dose of dexamethasone; Expert C calls it controversial; Expert A includes it as part of the initial bundle), the exact empiric antibiotic regimen (Expert A adds clindamycin to ceftriaxone for anaerobic/Staph coverage; Expert C suggests ceftriaxone alone unless β‑lactam allergy or MRSA risk; Expert B proposes ceftriaxone with optional vancomycin for MRSA), and post‑intubation management details such as sedation and neuromuscular blockade, timing and criteria for extubation, repeat imaging schedule, and prophylaxis for close contacts.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Portable pulse‑oximeter, capnograph, large‑bore intravenous catheters, bedside blood culture bottles, complete blood count with differential, lateral neck X‑ray (already obtained), full difficult‑airway cart including video‑laryngoscope or fiber‑optic bronchoscope, appropriately sized endotracheal tubes, suction device, surgical airway kit, and standard ICU monitoring equipment.  

Conclusion: Acute epiglottitis in a partially immunized 4‑year‑old with impending airway obstruction requiring immediate, controlled airway securement and broad‑spectrum antimicrobial therapy.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations: Position the child in a calm, semi‑upright (tripod) posture and administer supplemental oxygen only if it does not provoke agitation. Establish two large‑bore IV lines and begin isotonic fluid bolus to compensate for dehydration from drooling. Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics. Initiate IV ceftriaxone at 50–75 mg/kg every 24 h; add clindamycin 30 mg/kg every 6 h for anaerobic and Staphylococcus coverage if severe disease is suspected, or add vancomycin if local MRSA prevalence is high or the child has risk factors. Give a single dose of IV dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg if the clinical team decides steroids are indicated; otherwise, steroids may be omitted based on provider judgment.  

Call the most experienced pediatric anesthesiologist and ENT surgeon for rapid‑sequence intubation in the operating room or ICU, using video‑laryngoscopy or fiber‑optic bronchoscopy as the first line technique. Prepare the full difficult‑airway cart and have a surgical airway kit (cricothyrotomy or tracheostomy) ready. Avoid any oral or nasal airway examination, blind suctioning, or throat swabs until after the airway is secured to prevent laryngospasm.  

After successful intubation, provide continuous sedation and analgesia to prevent agitation; consider a short course of neuromuscular blockade only if required for ventilator synchrony, and titrate to the lowest effective dose. Maintain droplet isolation precautions until a definitive pathogen is identified, typically for at least 24 h after the start of appropriate antibiotics, and extend if cultures remain positive.  

Monitor airway edema with a repeat lateral neck X‑ray at 24–48 h, and be prepared for re‑intubation if clinical or radiographic signs of worsening swelling appear. Extubation should be considered only after resolution of stridor, stable oxygenation on minimal ventilatory settings, and a repeat endoscopic assessment confirming a patent airway; criteria include SpO₂ > 94 % on room air, no audible stridor, and the ability to handle secretions.  

Report the case to local public‑health authorities as a vaccine‑preventable Hib infection, and arrange for catch‑up immunizations before discharge. Offer rifampin chemoprophylaxis to household contacts who are not fully immunized, per public‑health guidelines. Provide thorough family counseling regarding the dangers of agitation, the importance of not attempting self‑removal of secretions, and the need for strict infection‑control measures.  

Conduct a multidisciplinary debrief after airway management to review performance, equipment readiness, and communication, and document lessons learned for future cases.  

Notes: Ensure all team members are briefed on the airway plan before arrival, double‑check that the surgical airway kit is functional, and keep a low‑threshold for converting to a surgical airway if intubation fails.

Complaint: Progressive periumbilical discomfort now localized to the right lower quadrant, decreased appetite, mild nausea, one loose stool; afebrile, mild tachycardia, mild leukocytosis.

Analysis: All three experts unanimously diagnosed acute appendicitis with early (contained) perforation based on the classic clinical migration of pain and the CT findings of a 14 mm dilated appendix, peri‑appendiceal fat stranding and a small localized fluid collection. Consensus also agreed that the condition is emergent and requires General Surgery involvement. Points of divergence included Expert A’s specific reminder to hold metformin and monitor for contrast‑induced nephropathy in a diabetic older adult, Expert B’s emphasis on a broader differential such as right‑sided diverticulitis or cecal carcinoma and the recommendation for a full metabolic and inflammatory panel, and Expert C’s brief mention of non‑operative management as a theoretical alternative, though this was not supported by the other two experts. These differences have been incorporated into the recommendations.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT (already performed), bedside electrocardiogram, cardiac enzymes (troponin), comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation profile, serum lactate, C‑reactive protein, complete blood count with differential, serum glucose and HbA1c, renal function (creatinine, eGFR) before and after contrast, urinalysis, and pre‑operative type and screen.

Conclusion: Acute appendicitis with early perforation.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery

Recommendations: Admit the patient to a monitored telemetry or step‑down unit; keep NPO; initiate vigorous intravenous crystalloid hydration to support renal perfusion and to mitigate contrast‑induced nephropathy; hold metformin for at least 48 hours after contrast exposure and resume only after renal function is confirmed stable. Begin empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics with coverage for gram‑negative and anaerobic organisms (e.g., piperacillin‑tazobactam or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole) and consider infectious disease consultation given the patient’s diabetes. Obtain urgent General Surgery consultation for definitive appendectomy; if the patient becomes hemodynamically unstable or an abscess forms, percutaneous drainage may be employed as a bridge to interval appendectomy. Conduct cardiac risk assessment—including ECG and troponin—maintain beta‑blockade if indicated, and provide continuous cardiac monitoring peri‑operatively. Implement tight peri‑operative glucose control with insulin as needed, and monitor for hyperglycemia‑related infection. Begin pharmacologic deep‑vein thrombosis prophylaxis and encourage early ambulation once medically feasible. Closely observe vital signs, heart rate, lactate trends, and abdominal examination for any signs of progression to generalized peritonitis. Re‑image with ultrasound or repeat CT only if clinical status deteriorates.

Notes: Elderly patients may lack fever or marked leukocytosis; a high index of suspicion and early imaging are crucial. Ensure post‑contrast renal function is rechecked before discharge. Document the decision‑making process regarding operative versus non‑operative pathways, acknowledging the higher recurrence risk with non‑operative management in this age group.

Treatment recommendations also vary: Expert A limits advice to ergonomic measures, Expert B adds artificial tears, preservative‑free options, and optional anti‑inflammatory drops or omega‑3 supplements, while Expert C emphasizes cycloplegic refraction for latent refractive error and suggests that persistent dry‑eye signs may merit targeted therapy.

Conclusion: The most likely diagnosis is Computer Vision Syndrome (digital eye strain) causing episodic eye fatigue, dryness, and tension‑type headache, a benign condition that is expected to improve with behavioral and environmental modifications.

Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology
Recommendations: Implement the 20‑20‑20 rule (every 20 minutes look at an object 20 feet away for 20 seconds), schedule regular micro‑breaks, optimise workstation ergonomics (monitor height at eye level, appropriate distance, anti‑glare screen, adequate ambient lighting), consciously increase blink rate, stay well hydrated, and use preservative‑free artificial tears several times daily. Expert C expressed low confidence and cautioned that an unrecognized low‑grade fever could be present, recommending objective temperature assessment. Apart from terminology, the diagnostic and therapeutic recommendations were largely aligned across experts.

Analysis: All three experts concur that the presentation is most consistent with papular urticaria, a hypersensitivity reaction to insect bites, most likely from mosquitoes or fleas. The morphology (pruritic erythematous papules with tiny central puncta) and the absence of systemic signs (fever, lymphangitis, respiratory distress) support this diagnosis and its classification as low‑urgency, self‑care appropriate. Minor points of divergence include the preferred topical agent (calamine lotion versus low‑potency 1 % hydrocortisone) and the level of detail in repellent safety instructions. All agree that routine laboratory testing is unnecessary unless atypical features develop. The panel also highlighted the need to inquire about pet/flea exposure, recent tick bites, and to provide comprehensive repellent education, issues not explicitly addressed in the original vignette but identified as important for comprehensive care.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: No routine tests are indicated. Consider skin scraping if scabies becomes a concern, bacterial culture if secondary infection appears, or serologic testing for Lyme disease only after a confirmed tick exposure or compatible evolving rash.
Conclusion: Papular urticaria secondary to insect bites; benign, self‑limited condition that can be managed with symptomatic treatment and preventive measures.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Provide oral non‑sedating antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine 5 mg once daily) for itch control. Apply a topical anti‑pruritic—either calamine lotion or 1 % hydrocortisone cream—2–3 times daily as tolerated. Use cool compresses, keep fingernails short, and consider cotton gloves at night to prevent excoriation and secondary bacterial infection. Ask the mother about recent pet contact, signs of flea infestation, and any known tick exposure; educate on regular tick checks after outdoor play. Instruct on proper use of EPA‑registered repellents (DEET 10‑30 % or picaridin 5‑20 % for children ≥2 months), applied to exposed skin and clothing, avoiding eyes, mouth, and broken skin, and reapplying per label after swimming or heavy sweating. Recommend wearing long sleeves/pants, reducing standing water around the home, and treating pets for fleas as needed. Advise follow‑up if lesions persist beyond two weeks, enlarge, become erythematous, suppurative, or if systemic symptoms such as fever, lymphadenopathy, or respiratory distress develop.
Notes: Monitor for signs of secondary infection (impetiginization) and for any large‑local or systemic hypersensitivity reactions. Educate caregivers on when to seek urgent care (e.g., fever, rapidly spreading cellulitis, wheezing, hypotension).

Analysis: The panel unanimously diagnosed acute pyelonephritis with systemic involvement, recognizing the high fever, rigors, tachycardia, borderline hypotension, and marked costovertebral angle tenderness as red‑flag signs of early sepsis. All experts agreed that Emergency Medicine should initiate care, while noting that early consultation with Urology or Infectious Disease may be warranted based on response or complications. Divergence existed in the emphasis on specialty leadership: Expert A and B prioritized Emergency Medicine with later involvement of Infectious Disease, whereas Expert C highlighted Infectious Disease as the primary managing service. Additionally, Experts B and C identified gaps in the initial questionnaire concerning allergy assessment, baseline renal function, definitive pregnancy testing, STI screening, and early evaluation for obstruction. These missing aspects were incorporated into the final recommendations.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urine dipstick and microscopy, urine culture with sensitivity, blood cultures, complete blood count with differential, basic metabolic panel including serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate, serum lactate, serum β‑hCG (quantitative) if any doubt about pregnancy, focused pelvic examination and STI testing as indicated, renal ultrasound as first‑line imaging for obstruction or abscess, non‑contrast CT abdomen/pelvis if ultrasound nondiagnostic or high suspicion for stones/abscess, vital sign monitoring, urine output measurement, and fluid status assessment (e.g., bedside ultrasound or physical exam).

Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with acute pyelonephritis complicated by systemic inflammatory response (possible sepsis) and requires emergent inpatient management.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency

Recommendations: Obtain a detailed medication and allergy history focusing on beta‑lactam and fluoroquinolone sensitivities before initiating antibiotics. Verify renal function (serum creatinine/eGFR) to guide antibiotic dosing and fluid management. Perform a quantitative serum β‑hCG to definitively exclude early pregnancy before imaging or antimicrobial choice. Conduct a brief pelvic examination and consider STI screening given recent sexual activity. Begin empiric intravenous ceftriaxone after cultures, adjusting to fluoroquinolone if local resistance is low and no beta‑lactam allergy, or to piperacillin‑tazobactam for broader coverage when resistant organisms are suspected or severe sepsis is evident. Initiate aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation guided by volume status assessment, monitor vital signs, urine output, and laboratory trends. Admit the patient for intravenous antibiotics, antipyretics, analgesia, and close observation, with re‑evaluation at 48 hours; if there is no clinical improvement, obtain renal ultrasound promptly and, if indicated, proceed to non‑contrast CT to evaluate for obstruction, hydronephrosis, or abscess. Engage Urology early if imaging reveals obstruction or abscess, and involve Infectious Disease for antimicrobial stewardship in the setting of prior UTIs and potential resistance. Consider prophylactic measures for thrombotic risk related to oral contraceptive use if immobilization becomes prolonged.

Notes: Prompt recognition of sepsis and early source control are critical. Re‑assessment of antibiotic regimen should occur once culture results and sensitivities are available. Patient education on signs of worsening infection and follow‑up after discharge is essential.

Sex: Male
Complaint: Burning and aching pain on the right side of the chest for 5 days, followed by erythema, a maculopapular rash that progressed to clusters of clear vesicles, then pustulation, ulceration, and crusting; associated headache and malaise.
Analysis: All three experts concur that the presentation is classic for herpes zoster (shingles) affecting a thoracic dermatome. The diagnosis is clinical; PCR or DFA of vesicle fluid is reserved for atypical or uncertain cases. Consensus agrees on prompt initiation of oral antiviral therapy within 72 hours of rash onset and that the case does not meet criteria for emergent care, though early treatment is important to reduce complications. Divergence arose regarding urgency (one expert initially suggested emergent evaluation, but the majority view it as non‑emergent) and the primary specialty (Dermatology versus Infectious Disease/General Medicine). Non‑pharmacologic skin care and a concrete follow‑up plan were added in the final round. Red‑flag signs (ocular involvement, neurologic deficits, high fever, rapid spread, secondary bacterial infection) were identified as triggers for escalation to urgent care.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required for routine diagnosis; optional vesicle fluid PCR/DFA if atypical. Baseline renal function tests to guide antiviral dosing; review vaccination history; assess immunocompromised status.
Conclusion: Herpes zoster (shingles) involving a right thoracic dermatome without current red‑flag features.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Initiate oral antiviral therapy (valacyclovir 1 g three times daily or famciclovir 500 mg three times daily) for 7 days as soon as possible, adjusting dose if renal impairment is present. Provide analgesia with acetaminophen or NSAIDs and consider neuropathic agents (gabapentin or pregabalin) for severe pain to lessen the risk of postherpetic neuralgia, especially given the patient’s age. Counsel the patient on skin care: keep lesions clean and dry, apply cool compresses, wear loose clothing, avoid scratching, and use loose dressings as needed. Monitor daily for signs of secondary bacterial infection (increasing pain, purulent discharge, expanding erythema) and for any red‑flag symptoms (eye involvement, neurologic changes, high fever, rapid rash spread); if any appear, seek urgent medical evaluation. Schedule a follow‑up visit in 1–2 weeks to assess lesion healing, pain control, and early indicators of postherpetic neuralgia. After complete crusting and healing, administer the recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) if the patient has not previously received it (2‑dose series, 2–6 months apart). Educate the patient about transmission risk to susceptible contacts (unvaccinated children, pregnant women, immunocompromised individuals) and advise temporary avoidance of close contact until lesions have crusted. If the rash were to involve the face or nasociliary distribution, arrange urgent ophthalmology review.
Notes: Age > 70, renal function, comorbidities (e.g., diabetes), and any immunosuppressive conditions modify antiviral dosing and complication risk. Vigilance for rare complications such as disseminated zoster or zoster meningitis is warranted in immunocompromised hosts.

Age: 28 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Continuous generalized tonic‑clonic seizure activity for >12 minutes despite pre‑hospital and emergency department benzodiazepines; associated fever, hypoxia, tachycardia, hypertension, irregular respirations, cyanosis.  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously identified the presentation as refractory (benzodiazepine‑resistant) convulsive status epilepticus requiring immediate life‑saving interventions and intensive‑care support. Consensus exists that emergency medicine should secure the airway, initiate rapid‑sequence intubation, and deliver a second‑line intravenous antiseizure medication, while neurology provides definitive seizure management and EEG interpretation. Minor divergences arose regarding the primary service: Expert A emphasized neurology as the lead for definitive care, whereas Experts B and C highlighted emergency medicine as the initial manager with urgent neurology consultation. Choice of second‑line agent also varied: Expert A and C listed levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate, and phenobarbital as options, advocating levetiracetam given prior use; Expert B preferentially recommended fosphenytoin based on rapid CNS penetration. These differences reflect acceptable therapeutic flexibility contingent on organ function, drug availability, and pregnancy status.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: rapid‑sequence intubation kit, video laryngoscope, endotracheal tubes, 100 % oxygen source, mechanical ventilator, pulse‑oximeter, capnography, invasive arterial line, cardiac telemetry monitor, continuous electroencephalography, point‑of‑care blood‑gas analyzer, complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, serum electrolytes (including Ca, Mg), renal and hepatic function panels, serum lactate, creatine kinase, ammonia, serum levetiracetam level, toxicology screen (serum and urine), blood cultures, non‑contrast head CT scanner, lumbar puncture tray (after imaging), pregnancy test, and appropriate IV fluids and vasoactive medications.  

Conclusion: The patient is experiencing refractory benzodiazepine‑resistant convulsive status epilepticus, most likely precipitated by recent levetiracetam non‑adherence, with secondary contributors including fever and autonomic instability. Immediate airway protection, second‑line antiseizure therapy, and ICU admission with continuous EEG are mandated.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Neurology  

Recommendations:  
1. Immediate rapid‑sequence intubation with 100 % oxygen, followed by controlled mechanical ventilation; secure suction equipment and apply invasive arterial blood‑pressure monitoring and cardiac telemetry.  
2. Administer a second‑line intravenous antiseizure medication without delay. Preferred agent should be chosen based on renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status, and drug‑interaction profile: (a) fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg load if hepatic function is adequate; (b) levetiracetam 60 mg/kg load if renal function is normal and prior tolerance is documented; (c) valproate or phenobarbital if contraindications to the first two exist.  
3. Transfer the patient to the intensive care unit for continuous EEG monitoring, strict neuro‑checks, and management of autonomic instability.  
4. Initiate the comprehensive laboratory and imaging work‑up listed above, including point‑of‑care ABG, CBC, CMP, electrolytes, CK, lactate, ammonia, levetiracetam level, toxicology screen, and blood cultures. Perform non‑contrast head CT emergently; if imaging excludes mass effect, proceed with lumbar puncture to evaluate for CNS infection.  
5. Monitor and treat systemic complications:  
   - Frequently reassess oxygenation and ventilation; treat aspiration risk and consider empiric antibiotics if pneumonia is suspected.  
   - Serial CK and renal function tests to detect rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury; initiate aggressive IV hydration as needed.  
   - Temperature management and evaluation of fever source (neurogenic vs infectious); obtain urine culture, chest imaging, and consider LP for meningitis/encephalitis.  
   - Cardiac monitoring for tachyarrhythmias; treat post‑ictal hypertension with short‑acting antihypertensives after seizure control.  
   - Verify pregnancy status; avoid valproate if pregnant.  
   - Screen for autoimmune encephalitis (serum/CSF antibodies) given the patient’s age and new‑onset provoked status.  
6. Address social determinants of health: involve social work immediately to resolve insurance barriers, arrange medication access, and plan outpatient follow‑up for medication adherence counseling.  
7. Document any traumatic injuries sustained during convulsions (tongue laceration, facial or skeletal trauma) and manage accordingly.  

Notes: The protocol allows flexibility in the choice of second‑line antiseizure medication while emphasizing rapid airway protection, definitive neurologic monitoring, and a broad diagnostic evaluation to identify and treat reversible precipitants. Collaboration between emergency medicine and neurology is essential, with emergency physicians leading stabilization and neurology directing ongoing seizure management and EEG interpretation.

Sex: Female  
Complaint: Six‑month history of bilateral milky nipple discharge, amenorrhea, daily headaches, weight gain, lethargy, decreased libido, and difficulty conceiving.  

Analysis: The constellation of galactorrhea, secondary amenorrhea, markedly elevated prolactin (500 µg/L), and a sellar mass measuring 1.1 × 1.6 × 2.1 cm on MRI is diagnostic of a prolactin‑secreting pituitary adenoma (macroprolactinoma). All three experts concur on this primary diagnosis and agree that the condition is non‑emergent but warrants timely endocrine evaluation. Consensus differs in nuances of medical therapy: Expert A favors cabergoline as the drug of choice and recommends continuation during pregnancy, while Expert B emphasizes bromocriptine’s longer safety record and suggests the option to discontinue medication in the first trimester; Expert B also highlights the need to discuss cabergoline‑associated valvulopathy. All experts agree that neurosurgical consultation is reserved for failure of medical therapy or acute compression. Additional considerations raised include screening for macroprolactin, assessing bone density due to prolonged hypoestrogenism, educating the patient on signs of pituitary apoplexy, monitoring blood pressure, addressing chronic NSAID use with gastro‑protective measures, and providing mental‑health support for mild depression.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Automated visual‑field testing (perimetry), serum macroprolactin assay (polyethylene‑glycol precipitation), comprehensive anterior‑pituitary hormone panel (LH, FSH, estradiol, morning cortisol, ACTH, free T4, TSH, IGF‑1), bone‑density scan (DXA), baseline renal and hepatic function tests, repeat contrast‑enhanced pituitary MRI at 3‑6 months, and routine blood‑pressure measurement.  

Conclusion: The patient has a macroprolactinoma presenting with hyperprolactinemia, galactorrhea, hypogonadism, and headache, without current visual‑field deficit or acute neuro‑ophthalmic emergency.

Age: 44  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Progressive nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain with refractory hypotension, electrolyte disturbances, and altered mental status in a patient with known Addison disease who has been unable to retain oral medications for 2 days.  

Analysis: The panel unanimously identified an acute adrenal (Addisonian) crisis precipitated by inability to absorb oral glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement during a viral gastroenteritis. All three experts agreed on the life‑threatening nature of the presentation, the red‑flag signs (refractory hypotension, hyper‑kalaemia with ECG changes, severe hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, AKI, altered mental status), and the need for immediate high‑dose IV hydrocortisone, aggressive fluid resuscitation, hyperkalaemia treatment, and ICU admission. Consensus was reached on the primary roles: Emergency Medicine leads initial stabilization, with urgent Endocrinology consultation and intensive‑care monitoring; fludrocortisone is withheld acutely because stress‑dose hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity.  

Points of divergence:  
- Expert A proposed a STAT ACTH stimulation test to confirm the diagnosis, whereas Experts B and C considered it unnecessary during the acute crisis and recommended postponing it until after stabilization.  
- Minor variation existed in the list of potential differentials (Expert B added adrenal haemorrhage; Expert A emphasized primary hyperkalaemic cardiac toxicity).  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Repeat basic metabolic panel (Na, K, Cl, HCO₃, BUN, creatinine, glucose), arterial or venous blood gas with lactate, 12‑lead ECG with continuous cardiac telemetry, bedside point‑of‑care glucose, serum cortisol (already drawn), rapid ACTH level if available (optional), blood cultures, urine output measurement, bedside ultrasound for volume status, and serum aldosterone if clinically indicated after stabilization.  

Conclusion: The patient is experiencing a severe primary adrenal insufficiency crisis with multi‑system decompensation that is not correctable with fluids alone. Immediate glucocorticoid replacement, volume resuscitation, electrolyte correction, and intensive monitoring are required to reverse shock and prevent fatal arrhythmias.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  

Recommendations:  
1. **Initial Stabilization** – Administer 100 mg IV hydrocortisone bolus immediately, followed by either a continuous infusion of 200 mg/24 h or 50 mg IV every 6–8 h until hemodynamic stability is achieved.  
2. **Fluid Resuscitation** – Give 1–2 L isotonic saline bolus rapidly; repeat as needed targeting MAP ≥ 65 mmHg. Add 5 % dextrose when glucose <70 mg/dL or to treat current hypoglycaemia.  
3. **Hyperkalaemia Management** – Initiate calcium gluconate IV, insulin‑glucose infusion, nebulised albuterol, and consider sodium bicarbonate if acidotic. Maintain continuous cardiac telemetry; prepare for emergent renal replacement therapy if K⁺ remains >6.5 mmol/L despite medical therapy.  
4. **Vasopressor Support** – Start norepinephrine infusion if MAP remains <65 mmHg after fluids and steroids.  
5. **Antibiotic Consideration** – Obtain blood cultures; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics empirically only if clinical or laboratory evidence suggests bacterial infection. Viral gastroenteritis alone does not mandate antibiotics.  
6. **Consultations** – Urgent Endocrinology consult, ICU admission for continuous hemodynamic, electrolyte, and cardiac monitoring. Involve Nephrology if renal replacement may be required, and Cardiology for ECG interpretation.  
7. **Diagnostic Testing** – Repeat BMP, glucose, ABG/lactate, ECG, and urine output hourly. Obtain ACTH level only if rapidly available and will alter immediate management; defer ACTH stimulation test until after crisis resolution.  
8. **Medication Review** – Review current medications for agents that may worsen renal hypoperfusion (e.g., ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs) and hold if appropriate.  
9. **Fludrocortisone** – Do not give during the acute phase; re‑introduce oral fludrocortisone once the patient is hemodynamically stable and tolerating oral intake.  
10. **Post‑acute Care** – Arrange outpatient Endocrinology follow‑up within 1 week. Adjust maintenance hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone doses based on repeat labs. Provide sick‑day rule education, an emergency injectable steroid kit, and counsel on early anti‑emetic use during future GI illnesses. Monitor electrolytes and renal function closely for the next 24–48 h.  

Notes: Hyperpigmentation reflects chronic ACTH excess and supports primary adrenal insufficiency. Hyponatraemia is multifactorial (mineralocorticoid loss, volume depletion, ADH excess). Renal impairment is likely prerenal but must be reassessed for possible progression.

winner_protocol:
Age: 20 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Itchy, peeling skin between the toes bilaterally for 2 weeks, associated with maceration and mild erythema in the third and fourth interdigital web spaces; no pain, swelling, or nail changes.  

Analysis: The panel converged on a diagnosis of interdigital tinea pedis (athlete’s foot) based on the classic presentation in a young athlete who uses communal showers, the bilateral maceration, peeling, and mild erythema confined to the web spaces, and the absence of vesicles, bullae, or nail involvement. All experts agreed the condition is uncomplicated and non‑urgent, suitable for outpatient management. Consensus also identified the primary differentials (candidal intertrigo, irritant/contact dermatitis, erythrasma, psoriasis/eczema, bacterial cellulitis) and highlighted red‑flag features that would warrant urgent care. Where the panel differed, Expert A classified the subclinical specialty as General Medicine (primary care) and suggested primary‑care alone is sufficient, whereas Experts B and C assigned Dermatology as the appropriate sub‑specialty, reserving referral for refractory or atypical cases. Expert C also labeled the emergency type as “Self‑care appropriate,” while the majority and final consensus label the case as requiring non‑emergent care.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Visual inspection of the feet; potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of skin scrapings if diagnostic uncertainty arises; Wood’s lamp examination if erythrasma is suspected; fungal culture optional for treatment‑failure work‑up or atypical pathogen identification.  

Conclusion: Interdigital tinea pedis, uncomplicated, non‑urgent.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  

Recommendations: Initiate topical antifungal therapy with terbinafine 1 % cream applied once daily to the affected web spaces for 1–2 weeks; azole creams such as clotrimazole are acceptable alternatives if terbinafine is unavailable. Emphasize strict moisture control: keep feet dry, change socks at least daily, use absorbent or antifungal powder in shoes and on feet, wear breathable moisture‑wicking footwear, and avoid walking barefoot in communal showers. Advise regular shoe rotation, disinfection of footwear and locker‑room equipment, and use of prophylactic antifungal powder in shoes or socks to reduce recurrence. Counsel the patient on the impact of athletic training schedules on adherence and encourage application of the topical agent after showering and before training sessions when feasible. Schedule a follow‑up visit in 2–3 weeks to assess clinical response and adherence. Educate the patient to monitor for nail changes (thickening, discoloration, onycholysis) and to report any such findings promptly; early detection may require oral antifungal therapy. Instruct the patient to watch for red‑flag signs of bacterial superinfection—including increased pain, swelling, warmth, purulent discharge, fever, or lymphangitis—and to seek prompt medical evaluation if they occur; mild bacterial overgrowth may be managed with topical antiseptics, whereas cellulitis warrants oral antibiotics (e.g., cephalexin). If there is no improvement after appropriate topical therapy, reassess adherence, obtain KOH (or culture if needed) to confirm the organism, consider atypical dermatophytes, and refer to dermatology for possible oral antifungal treatment and further work‑up.  

Notes: Consider assessment of other body sites (groin, torso) for concurrent dermatophyte infection; clean or avoid shared towels, locker‑room floors, and gym equipment to minimise environmental reservoirs.
